questiontext.text: In an undirected graph, an edge between vertices u and v is best described as which of the following?

answer.text: An unordered pair {u, v} that can be traversed in either direction

feedback.text: Correct — undirected edges have no direction, so {u, v} = {v, u}.

answer.text: An ordered pair (u, v) that can only be traversed from u to v

feedback.text: That describes a directed edge (arc), not an undirected edge.

answer.text: A self-loop that always connects a vertex to itself

feedback.text: A self-loop is a special case, not the general definition of an edge.

answer.text: A weight value assigned to a single vertex

feedback.text: Edges connect two vertices; they are not vertex weights.

generalfeedback.text: An undirected edge is an unordered pair {u, v}; it can be crossed both ways and is the same as {v, u}.

questiontext.text: The degree of a vertex in an undirected graph is defined as:

answer.text: The number of edges incident to that vertex

feedback.text: Correct — degree counts the edges touching the vertex.

answer.text: The number of vertices in the whole graph

feedback.text: That is V, not the degree of one vertex.

answer.text: The length of the longest path starting at that vertex

feedback.text: That is unrelated to degree.

answer.text: The total number of edges E in the graph

feedback.text: That is the edge count, not a single vertex's degree.

generalfeedback.text: A vertex's degree is simply how many edges are incident to it.

questiontext.text: By the handshaking lemma, the sum of the degrees of all vertices in an undirected graph with E edges equals:

feedback.text: Correct — each edge contributes 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints.
Each edge is counted once per endpoint, so the total is twice E.
The number of vertices is unrelated to the degree sum.
The sum is larger than E, not smaller.

generalfeedback.text: Every edge adds 1 to the degree of each endpoint, so the degrees sum to 2E (handshaking lemma).

questiontext.text: Which term names a path that starts and ends at the same vertex without repeating any edge?

feedback.text: Correct — a closed path returning to its start is a cycle.
A subgraph is any subset of vertices and edges, not specifically a closed path.
A spanning tree is acyclic and connects all vertices; it has no cycle.
Degree counts incident edges, not a path.

generalfeedback.text: A cycle is a closed path that returns to its starting vertex without reusing an edge.

questiontext.text: An undirected graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices.

feedback.text: Correct — connectivity means every pair of vertices is joined by some path.
By definition, a connected graph has a path between any two vertices.

questiontext.text: In an undirected graph, the edge {u, v} is different from the edge {v, u}.

feedback.text: They are the same unordered pair; undirected edges have no direction.
Correct — {u, v} and {v, u} denote the same undirected edge.

questiontext.text: The number of edges incident to a vertex in an undirected graph is called its ______.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about undirected graphs are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: The sum of all vertex degrees equals 2E

feedback.text: Yes — the handshaking lemma.

answer.text: A subgraph consists of a subset of the vertices and edges of the graph

feedback.text: Yes — that is the definition of a subgraph.

answer.text: Every edge must be traversed in one fixed direction only

feedback.text: No — undirected edges can be crossed either way.

answer.text: The degree of a vertex always equals V

feedback.text: No — degree depends on incident edges, not the vertex count.

generalfeedback.text: Undirected graphs: degrees sum to 2E, subgraphs are subsets, edges are bidirectional, and degree counts incident edges (not V).
